title: UN Warns 300,000 People Trapped in Asian Scam Centres as Trafficking Surges
excerpt: The IOM says victims from India, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka are among those lured by fake job ads on social media and forced into criminal operations across Cambodia, Laos and Myanmar.
body:
• An estimated 300,000 people are trapped in scam compounds across Cambodia, Laos and Myanmar, according to IOM Director General Amy Pope
  • Victims from India, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and over 80 countries are targeted with fake job advertisements on social media
  • A separate UNODC report estimates scam operations caused $88.3 billion to $114.1 billion in losses across Asia-Pacific in 2025
  • Criminal syndicates are using AI, deepfakes and encrypted platforms to expand operations globally, with children increasingly at risk

The UN's International Organization for Migration on Tuesday sounded the alarm on a dramatic surge in human trafficking into online scam centres across Southeast Asia, with an estimated 300,000 people now caught up in illicit call centre networks largely based in Cambodia, Laos and Myanmar.

IOM Director General Amy Pope, speaking in Geneva, said victims from Bangladesh, India, Indonesia, Sri Lanka, Ethiopia and Kenya are being targeted with fake advertisements — often on social media — promising lucrative employment for people with strong English skills and university degrees.

"People trapped in scam compounds are victims of trafficking. We're seeing so many more of these cases emerge right now."

— Amy Pope, IOM Director General

Inside the Compounds

Once lured in, victims are stripped of their travel documents and forced to carry out online schemes designed to defraud often older Westerners of money, according to the IOM. Some of those trafficked are also sexually abused. Pope estimates that tens of thousands of people from over 80 countries have been trafficked into these operations.

https://x.com/Reuters/status/2082149445475377610

Even escape offers no guarantee of safety. Pope said that when individuals manage to flee or are freed in government raids, many still face prosecution for participating in criminal activity — compounding the trauma of their exploitation.

"The significant networks are based within Asia, but because of social media… because of the ability to now reach people in many, many countries… their reach has expanded quite significantly," Pope said, according to TBS News.

A Multi-Billion Dollar Criminal Economy

The IOM's warning came days after a separate report from the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime painted an even broader picture of the crisis. The UNODC estimated that scam operations caused between $88.3 billion and $114.1 billion in losses across East Asia, Southeast Asia, Australia and New Zealand in 2025 alone — a figure larger than the GDP of several nations in the region.

Nearly three-quarters of scam compounds are located in the Mekong region, according to the UNODC, with satellite imagery revealing operations spanning over 500 acres. But the criminal networks are spreading. Operations have expanded to the Pacific Islands, South Asia, Gulf States, West Africa and the Americas.

"Their operating model looks like corporate franchising: imagine specialised departments for laundering money, trafficking people, smuggling migrants, and harvesting data, all plugged into the same, service-based interconnected network."

— Delphine Schantz, UNODC Regional Representative for Southeast Asia and the Pacific

Chinese syndicates constitute the major organisational force behind the region's scam economy, running industrial-scale compounds in border areas and special economic zones in Myanmar, Cambodia and Laos, the UNODC report found.

AI and the Growing Threat to Children

Criminal groups are harnessing artificial intelligence and encrypted platforms to scale their operations, using generative AI to create convincing phishing content, deploy real-time deepfake videos, and target victims across multiple languages simultaneously, according to the AP.

Children are increasingly at risk. The UNODC report flagged a sharp rise in AI-generated child sexual abuse material communicated through encrypted platforms. "There is a huge jump in AI-generated child sexual images," said Inshik Sim, UNODC researcher and coordinator for the report.

The Indian Diaspora Connection

India is explicitly named among the countries whose citizens are most frequently targeted by trafficking networks. Indians with English-language fluency and technical skills are particularly vulnerable to fake job advertisements that promise high-paying roles abroad. South Asian recruitment networks operate through transit hubs across the region, the Middle East and Africa, making the pipeline from India to scam compounds disturbingly efficient. The crisis adds urgency to calls from Indian consular authorities and diaspora organisations for greater awareness among young job-seekers considering overseas opportunities.

What's Next

The IOM called for continued support to assist trafficking victims through protection, safe return and reintegration, while scaling up public awareness of traffickers' tactics. Myanmar's military-backed parliament, meanwhile, approved an "Anti-Online Scam Bill" on Tuesday authorising severe punishment — including execution — for those who use violence or unlawful detention to force others into scam operations.

But crackdowns have had limited effect. As authorities in Thailand, China and elsewhere have raided scam centres, criminal groups have responded by shifting to smaller-scale operations, moving to villas and other properties, and expanding to new geographies. "They were destroyed, but none of the operations stopped," said Seong Jae Shin, an analyst at the UNODC.
nri_angle: Indians are explicitly named among the nationalities most targeted by trafficking networks, with English-fluent, university-educated job-seekers particularly vulnerable to fake employment ads funnelling them into scam compounds across Southeast Asia.
